title: Speculative decoding
summary: A cheap draft proposes several tokens and the large model verifies them in one pass. Accepted tokens come at the price of one step, and the output distribution stays the same.
useIf: You run your own model, single-stream decode speed matters, and load is low to medium so the GPU is memory-bound with spare compute.
avoidIf: The GPU is saturated by large batches, or the draft agrees with the target too rarely to pay for itself.

explain.md: Decode generates one token per step and is memory-bandwidth-bound, so compute sits idle. **Speculative decoding** uses that spare compute. A cheap **draft** proposes a few tokens. The large **target** model scores all of them in a single parallel pass, keeps the longest prefix it agrees with and samples one more token itself. The paper shows the output distribution is unchanged and reports 2x to 3x faster decoding on T5-XXL with identical outputs [[r19]].

steps.title: Draft
steps.md: The draft proposes k tokens cheaply.

steps.title: Verify
steps.md: The target scores all k in one parallel pass.

steps.title: Accept
steps.md: Keep the agreeing prefix, resample the first disagreement.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.md: Continue from the new end of the text.

explain.title: Expected tokens per target pass

vars.v: acceptance rate, the chance a drafted token is accepted (assumed independent)
number of drafted tokens per step

explain.example: With a = 0.8 and k = 4: (1 - 0.8^5) / 0.2 = 3.36 tokens per target pass. With a = 0.5 it is 1.94. A drafter that is cheap but rarely right gains little. Formula from the speculative decoding paper [[r19]].

explain.md: **Variants.** A separate draft model, EAGLE (which drafts at the feature level instead of the token level [[tr9]]), multi-token prediction heads on the target itself, and lightweight n-gram or suffix methods that need no extra model. vLLM enables them through `--speculative-config` with a `method` and `num_speculative_tokens`. Its documentation says speculation reduces inter-token latency under medium-to-low QPS, memory-bound workloads, that model-based methods give the best latency reduction, and that n-gram and suffix methods give modest speedups without adding workload during peak traffic [[tr18]].

explain.title: The hosted cousin
explain.md: OpenAI's latency guide suggests Predicted Outputs when most of the output is already known, for example a small edit to a large document [[r15]].

whereToUse: Interactive self-hosted assistants at low to medium load, where per-user speed is the goal
Code editing and document revision, where output copies much of the input
Large target models whose single-stream decode is slow
Workloads with a good small draft from the same model family
Edit-in-place tasks on hosted APIs through Predicted Outputs

use: Decode is memory-bound and GPUs have spare compute at your load
Outputs are predictable enough for a draft to agree often
Exact output equivalence matters, since the distribution is unchanged
avoid: GPUs run at high batch saturation, where verification competes for real compute
The draft model rarely agrees, as in highly creative, high-entropy text
You have no memory left for a draft model and no lightweight method fits
flips: Traffic grows and batches saturate: gains shrink, so switch to a lighter method or turn it off
No good draft exists: use n-gram or suffix methods for repetitive outputs
You need maximum throughput, not per-user speed: spend effort on batching and quantization first

pitfalls.symptom: Speculation made throughput worse at peak
pitfalls.cause: Batches are saturated, so verifying drafted tokens costs real compute
pitfalls.fix: Use a lighter method or disable it above a load threshold, and measure at peak traffic [[tr18]]

pitfalls.symptom: Little speedup although speculation is on
pitfalls.cause: Low acceptance rate because the draft diverges from the target
pitfalls.fix: Pick a better-matched draft or EAGLE head, lower k, and watch acceptance metrics [[r19]]

pitfalls.symptom: Out-of-memory after enabling a draft model
pitfalls.cause: The draft weights and KV take memory from the target's cache
pitfalls.fix: Account for draft memory in capacity planning, or choose a method without a separate model

scenarios.title: Code assistant at modest load
scenarios.situation: A team self-hosts a large code model for an editor plugin. Load is moderate. Users edit existing files, so output copies a lot of input. Streams run at 20 tokens per second and users want faster.
unknowns: Is a matched small draft or EAGLE head available?
How much GPU memory is free?
scenarios.question: Which lever do you try first?

options.name: Spend on larger batches and more GPUs
options.tradeoff: It does not make a single stream faster, which is the complaint.

options.name: Enable speculative decoding with a matched draft or EAGLE head
options.why: Decode is memory-bound at this load, copy-heavy output gives high acceptance, and the output is unchanged.
options.tradeoff: Needs extra memory and tuning of the number of drafted tokens.

options.name: Quantize KV to 2 bits
options.why: KV quantization is for memory capacity, not single-stream speed, and carries quality risk.
options.tradeoff: Right when KV memory caps concurrency.

flips.then: Expect smaller gains and test turning it off at peak.
Try n-gram or suffix speculation, which suit copy-heavy output.

scenarios.takeaway: Speculation speeds single streams when decode has idle compute.

scenarios.title: Saturated fleet, cost pressure
scenarios.situation: A high-traffic service keeps its GPUs at near full batch occupancy all day. Per-user speed is acceptable. Finance wants a lower cost per token. A teammate proposes adding a draft model.
constraints: Goal is cost per token, not single-stream speed
unknowns: What is the batch occupancy at peak?
Is memory free for a draft model?
scenarios.question: What do you recommend?

options.name: Add a model-based draft for speed
options.why: At saturation there is little spare compute, so verification competes with real work and a draft model takes memory.
options.tradeoff: Right at low to medium load where decode leaves compute idle.

options.name: Look at weight quantization and batching efficiency
options.why: These raise tokens per GPU hour, which is the cost metric, and they do not rely on idle compute.
options.tradeoff: Quantization needs an eval gate for quality.

options.name: Try n-gram or suffix speculation
options.why: The docs describe modest gains without extra workload at peak traffic.
options.tradeoff: Gains are small, and only for repetitive output.

flips.if: Traffic drops overnight to low load
flips.then: Enable model-based speculation during the quiet window.

flips.if: A latency SLO for single streams is added
flips.then: Revisit speculation with a measured threshold.

scenarios.takeaway: Match the optimisation to the metric: speed for one user, or cost across many.

quiz.q: A drafter has acceptance rate 0.8 and proposes 4 tokens per step. Using E = (1 - a^(k+1)) / (1 - a), how many tokens does one target pass yield on average?
quiz.explain: (1 - 0.32768) / 0.2 = 3.36. At acceptance 0.5 the same formula gives about 1.94, so a draft that agrees less often gains much less.

quiz.q: What does speculative decoding do to the distribution of the generated text?
options: It leaves it unchanged, because the target verifies every drafted token
It slightly shifts it toward the draft model
It lowers quality in exchange for speed
quiz.explain: Rejection-based verification makes the output distribution identical to sampling from the target alone. The speedup comes from computing several tokens in parallel, not from approximating.

quiz.q: Which conditions shrink the benefit of speculative decoding?
options: GPUs saturated by large batches at high QPS
A low acceptance rate between draft and target
Copy-heavy output with an n-gram method
quiz.explain: Saturation removes the spare compute that verification uses, and low acceptance wastes drafted tokens. Memory-bound low load and copy-heavy output are where speculation helps.

flashcards.front: How does speculative decoding keep outputs identical?
flashcards.back: The target verifies all drafted tokens in one pass, keeps the agreeing prefix and resamples the first disagreement, so the distribution is unchanged.

flashcards.front: When does speculation help most, and when does it fade?
flashcards.back: It helps at low to medium QPS in memory-bound decode. Gains shrink as batches saturate or acceptance falls.
A speculative sampling method that drafts at the feature level (second-to-top-layer features) instead of the token level.
